stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Sweep all three sliders to see how the gravitational attraction $F$ between two bodies depends on each mass and their separation. Advance once each slider has covered at least half its range.
stages.concept: Newton's law of universal gravitation: $F = G\,\dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$ with $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$. $F$ scales linearly with either mass and falls as $1/r^2$ with separation. Same $1/r^2$ shape as Coulomb's law — the physics of central forces.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A target force magnitude $|F^*|$ is shown. Adjust $m_1$, $m_2$, and $r$ until the live force arrow matches the dashed target arrow. Many triples produce the same force.
stages.concept: $F$ has three degrees of freedom, so infinitely many $(m_1, m_2, r)$ triples yield the same $|F^*|$. Fixing any two of the three constrains the third: $r = \sqrt{G\,m_1 m_2 / |F^*|}$.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: Force arrows are hidden. Only the target $|F^*|$ is shown. Compute a valid $(m_1, m_2, r)$ triple on paper, then set the sliders to your values and submit. One submit per setup — a miss rotates to a new target.
stages.concept: Rearrange the formula: pick two of the three parameters (typical: fix $m_1$ near an Earth-mass value $\sim 6\times 10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $m_2$ near a satellite value), then solve $r = \sqrt{G\,m_1 m_2 / |F^*|}$. Convert back to slider units — the sliders show $m_1$ in $10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2$ in $10^{22}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $r$ in $\mathrm{Mm}$.

labels.tip1: sweep m1, m2, r each across at least half their range
labels.tip2: match the force arrow to the dashed target arrow
labels.tip3: compute a valid (m1, m2, r) on paper, then set sliders
labels.peek_tip_formula: Rearrange: r = sqrt(G · m1 · m2 / F*). Fix m1 near 6 (Earth) and m2 near 10, then solve r.
labels.peek_tip_anchor: In slider units: F [N] = 6.67e23 · m1 · m2 / r_Mm². Cross-check by order of magnitude first.

1.1: The force depends on THREE parameters — each slider changes the arrow differently. Which changes it fastest?
1.2: Doubling m1 or m2 doubles the force. Doubling r divides the force by four.
1.3: The 1/r^2 dependence dominates — a small change in r shifts F much more than a small change in either mass.

2.1: Read the target |F*| in the top-right HUD. Which combination of sliders would produce that magnitude?
2.2: Fix two parameters at round values, then solve for the third. For example, keep m1 = 6 and r = 100 Mm, then find m2.
2.3: F = G · m1 · m2 / r². Isolate: m2 = F · r² / (G · m1). Plug in your target and your two chosen values.

3.1: The visualization is gone by design — you must compute. Write Newton's formula on paper and identify what's known.
3.2: The sliders are in scaled units. The full formula in slider units is F [N] = 6.67 × 10^23 · m1 · m2 / r_Mm² — much simpler than the raw SI form.
3.3: Pick a round value for m1 (say 6 or 10), and another for m2 (say 5 or 20). Then solve r = sqrt(6.67e23 · m1 · m2 / F*) directly — no unknowns left.
